questions.q: Why does the summary say interruption marketing no longer works?
a: People's attention is too overloaded to notice ads
Advertisers can no longer afford television spots
Consumers now trust large brands more than before
Regulators have restricted how often ads may run
questions.why: Lesson 1 says we see so many ads that our brains simply refuse to pay attention to any of them.

questions.q: What are the three steps of permission marketing?
a: Make an offer, build a relationship, then ask for a sale
Buy attention, repeat the message, then close quickly
Collect data, segment the list, then sell the data
Run an ad, measure the clicks, then raise the budget
questions.why: Lesson 2 lays out the sequence: invite people with a unique offer, talk with them regularly, then ask for a sale.

questions.q: Why is permission marketing described as far more effective?
a: The people it reaches have opted in and are likelier to buy
It reaches a much larger audience than television did
It costs more per person, which signals quality
It removes the need to make any initial contact
questions.why: Lesson 2 says the audience is far more likely to buy because they expressed interest voluntarily.

questions.q: According to the summary, what always comes along with permission?
a: A mission to keep the promise you made
A contract that locks in the relationship
A fee paid for each new subscriber
An exclusive claim on the customer's attention
questions.why: Lesson 3 says that with permission comes a mission, so a promised coupon or ebook has to be delivered.

questions.q: What promise does the Four Minute Books homepage make to subscribers?
a: Seven new book summaries every Saturday
One new book summary every weekday
Five summaries delivered every Sunday
A monthly review of the best new books
questions.why: Lesson 3 quotes the homepage promise of seven new summaries each Saturday, and says it is kept.
